extracted.intended_audience: CRTC staff, broadcasters, provincial regulators, broadcasting lawyers, and administrative law policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria governing CRTC broadcasting licensing: jurisdictional constraints, application processing, notice/intervention rules, hearing formats, licensing conditions, and enforcement practices as described in a Law Reform Commission study of the CRTC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of double licensing and conflicting regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Double licensing (provincial and federal) imposes increased costs, duplicate applications and conflicting regulatory requirements on operators and forces choice between authorities' requirements, risking disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experience in Quebec demonstrated the disadvantages of a double licensing system: duplicate licence fees, increased costs, and conflicting regulatory requirements that place operators in an unenviable position. Jurisdictional resolution (e.g., Supreme Court decisions) can remove these burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee ownership/control of cable physical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRTC traditionally requires that cable licensees maintain some degree of control over the physical elements of their undertakings (minimum: receiving antenna, amplifiers, drop wires).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy has conflicted with provincially owned telephone companies that insist on owning the entire distribution system and leasing capacity; such conflicts can prevent applicants from completing applications 'to the satisfaction of the CRTC' and create jurisdictional struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation of channel(s) for educational programming upon provincial request
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet direction (pursuant to section 26) requires cable licensees to reserve at least one channel for educational programming purposes when so requested by a provincial authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This direction was issued in 1970 to accommodate provincial interest in educational broadcasting. It has been implemented as a licensing condition and affects channel allocation on cable systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility criteria for 'independent corporations' licensed for educational broadcasting
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1972 a Cabinet direction permitted the Commission to issue licences to 'independent corporations' defined as corporations the CRTC is satisfied are not directly controlled by provincial or municipal governments and are designated for educational programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such corporations have been licensed in Ontario, Quebec and Alberta. The designation requires both independence from direct government control and a commitment to educational programming as described in the direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence safeguards for provincially funded educational stations
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing the 'independence' of provincially funded educational corporations can be difficult where legislation makes the corporation's dealings subject to directions by a provincial authority (e.g., Alberta Educational Communications Corporation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CRTC views such direction power as a potential for direct government interference with the Corporation's independence, and licensing decisions have voiced concern about this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of 'educational' stations entering general entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a regulatory problem when 'educational' stations enter general entertainment broadcasting, because the cabinet direction’s loose definition permits programming 'distinctly different from general broadcasting' to be stretched to movies and dramas of wide appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private broadcasters' complaints have been of little avail due to the loose definition. The CRTC finds it difficult to challenge the educational value of programming given provincial jurisdiction over education and thus faces a programming-regulation jurisdictional dilemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRTC broad discretionary powers to implement broadcasting policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Broadcasting Act vests broad powers in the CRTC to regulate and supervise broadcasting with a view to implementing policy objectives in Section 3; sections 16 and 17 grant regulation-making and licence-condition powers 'as the Executive Committee deems appropriate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act's broad language allows expansive exercise of discretion; courts have supported broad interpretations in challenges. Section 17 expressly permits attaching conditions 'as the Executive Committee deems appropriate' for policy implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licence term, renewal, suspension and revocation as oversight tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The maximum term for a broadcasting licence is five years; the CRTC may suspend or revoke licences and may choose not to renew licences if performance is found wanting, though suspension/revocation and non-renewal have been rarely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five-year maximum provides an opportunity for periodic review of licensee performance; in practice revocation/suspension are exceptional while renewal monitoring is the common oversight mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval requirements for transfers of ownership and share transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard licence conditions require prior CRTC approval for all share transfers in companies whose shares are not publicly traded; for publicly traded companies the requirement applies only to transfers of effective control of the undertaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction recognizes realities of public securities trading and seeks to avoid excessive regulatory intrusion into market trading while maintaining control over changes in effective control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-making via published proposals and public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRTC actively formulates policy principles as guides to licensing decisions and publishes these as white papers, allowing public and broadcasters to comment on proposed policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing policy proposals and inviting comment helps create a more certain and consistent regulatory environment and guides the Commission's discretionary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints handling and licensee accountability for programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Broadcasting Act responsibility for programs rests with licensees; the CRTC generally refers complaints to the licensee to reply directly to complainants and keeps a record of complaints that may affect licence renewal; it has power to hold public hearings on complaints but rarely does so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CRTC expects licensees to be accountable to the public and to resolve programming complaints. A record of complaints is maintained and may influence renewal decisions; formal public hearings on complaints are exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for technical briefs and Department of Communications certification
rubrics_metrics.description: For new licences and certain applications a technical brief must accompany the application and the Minister of Communications must certify that the applicant satisfies the Radio Act requirements and will be issued a 'technical construction and operating certificate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No licence may be issued, amended or renewed unless the Department certifies technical compliance; the technical brief is routed to the Department of Communications as part of processing prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional licensing superintendents' role in application processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Each regional licensing superintendent has primary responsibility for shepherding applications from their region through analysis to decision, overseeing analyses, obtaining branch comments, requesting additional information, deciding on hearings, briefing Commissioners, acting as secretary at hearings, and assisting in preparing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These responsibilities create a heavy load on superintendents who also administer branches and maintain liaison with broadcasters; the role is central to coordinating application processing and public access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limitations of 'hearing manager' system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission experimented with appointing a 'hearing manager' for each hearing who would assemble a cross-branch team to analyze applications, prepare comments, audit the hearing and prepare post-hearing analyses; the system has been abandoned due to operational difficulties and commissioner availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hearing manager was selected based on the predominant nature of the agenda (e.g., Programs Branch member for FM renewals). While the system expedited hearings and localized panels, it removed responsibilities from superintendents and faced staffing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of hearing agendas into 'appearing' and 'non-appearing' items
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are divided into 'appearing' and 'non-appearing' items; designation depends on whether interventions raise significant issues or whether the application itself raises such issues (e.g., revocation, suspension, change of control vs routine renewals or minor technical changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-appearing items are used where licensees perform satisfactorily and no serious complaints exist; examples of non-appearing items include transmitter site changes and small territory additions. Appearing items include change of control, significant programming format changes, renewals with serious complaints, or substantial rate changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of applications and hearing scheduling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 20 requires notice in the Canada Gazette of any application for issue/amendment/renewal of a broadcasting licence and of any public hearing; the Commission's Rules require Gazette notice not less than 50 days before the hearing and notice in local newspapers and on-air (licensees must broadcast notice during prime time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices must be published in one or more newspapers of general circulation within the area served/proposed to be served, and the 50-day Gazette timeline guides intervention and scheduling windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention procedure and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices state that interested parties may intervene to support, oppose or seek modifications during a period up to 20 days prior to the commencement of the hearing; intervention is accomplished by serving a copy on the applicant and filing it with proof of service with the CRTC; applicants may reply within 10 days (discretionary) or respond orally at the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants' 10-day written reply right is discretionary; regardless, applicants may address interventions orally at the public hearing whether or not a written reply was filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefing materials for Commissioners (factum book)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'factum book' for Commissioners contains summaries of applications, licensing histories, branch comments raising issues (financing, programming, ownership), suggested questions for applicants, and references to relevant regulations or policy statements; Commissioners rely primarily on this book and receive an oral briefing the day before hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factum book is an important preparatory tool; oral briefings by the public hearing secretary supplement written materials immediately prior to hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing format and evidentiary practice in broadcasting matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRTC employs an informal hearing format similar to a debate: applicants make oral presentations (often reading prepared texts), are questioned by Commissioners and Commission Counsel; interveners then present; evidence is not sworn and there is no cross-examination beyond Commission questioning; departures (e.g., cross-examination) occur in revocation or non-renewal cases where facts must be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where licence loss is possible (revocation or non-renewal), more formal procedures including sworn evidence and cross-examination may be used to ensure precision and testing of facts; otherwise, proceedings are informal with no leading of evidence by applicants' counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition rules and role of part-time members
rubrics_metrics.description: Public hearings may be chaired by as few as two members (one must be full‑time), though practice has used larger panels historically; part-time members are appointed regionally, participate in broadcasting matters and may chair panels but lack power to make final licensing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With more numerous hearings, panels rarely exceed three or four members; part-time members represent the province where hearing is held and can play important roles despite lacking final decision voting power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional organization of hearings to facilitate local access
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission attempts to organize hearings on a regional basis so that matters heard locally primarily concern undertakings in that province, and experiments with smaller, localized panels facilitate public access to hearings in smaller communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller panels and localized hearings speed consideration of applications and improve public access; however, implementing such systems depends on commissioner availability and operational capacity.
